content.text:
Yes, but there's no structured "choice" field. The chips come from a plain-text line at the end of the agent's reply.

- **The prompt:** the `CHOICES` instruction in [printerInstructions.ts:76](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts:76) tells the model to end any yes/no, confirm, or pick-one question with a last line like `Choices: Yes, that is it | Different printer`. That means two to four answers, each under 30 characters, with nothing after the line. The filament chat uses the same text ([filamentInstructions.ts:52](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts:52)).
- **The parsing:** `splitChoices` in [replyChoices.ts:21](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/replyChoices.ts:21) looks only at the last line. It finds `Choices:` wherever it starts a word, so `Set it to 0.6? Choices: Yes | Not yet` on one line also works. It splits on `|` and removes that part from the text shown in the message.
- **While the reply is streaming:** `withoutPartialChoices` hides a trailing `C`, `Ch`, … `Choices: …` so the line never flashes up as text before it becomes chips.
- **The chips:** [MessageList.tsx:290](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/components/MessageList.tsx:290) shows them only on the newest finished assistant message. Once any later message arrives, including the person's own, the older chips go away. Tapping a chip sends its text as the person's own message.

If the model leaves the line out, the reply is just text and the person types an answer.

# Project chat prompt tests

The project chat's assistant is a system prompt
(`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`), the 27 project
tools and the chat. `run_prompt_tests.py` asks the live model for its next
step at a known point of a project chat and checks that step against one
sentence of the prompt. It is run against the prompt before an edit and after it, and the
counts compared. The app does not run.

On Kenneth's local machine, the keys are in
`~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env` (outside the repository, mode `600`). An
agent running this suite can load them for that command in a subshell:

```bash
( . "$HOME/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env"; tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py )
```

Do not print, copy into the repository, or include the key values in a command
or test log. The file exports `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`; the
runner reads them from its environment. No run happens without Kenneth
approving that batch (case count, runs, token estimate). A `403 Key limit
exceeded` means stop; do not switch keys.

The model, hosts and judge are the printer suite's (`tests/printer_prompt`,
"Which model"): DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, pinned to Alibaba,
Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud, with a pinned OpenAI judge. `--backend
claude-cli` runs the same cases on the developer's Claude subscription
instead, for iterating on a prompt without API cost (see "Running on the
Claude subscription").

## One step, with its reads answered

Each case starts at a point recorded from the app and judges the model's next
step: a reply, or its tool calls. One response may hold several calls. The
app asks for that (`parallel_tool_calls: true`) and runs every call in the
order the model wrote it, so every call is judged here:

- A change anywhere in the response (any call the registry does not mark
  read-only) is the step, whatever came before it; the first change if
  there are several. It ends the run, and nothing is answered.
- A response of reads only is checked read by read, in order, and the first
  read the case decides on is the outcome: `issue-fix` passes on a
  `settings_get` of its setting sent after a `workspace_inspect`.
- When the case decides on none of the reads (such as `workspace_inspect`
  before a reply), every one is answered with the result the app gave for
  that read at the same point, each under its own call id, and the model is
  asked again, at most three times (`MAX_READS`, counted in responses). As
  the app does, a read after one whose result did not succeed gets the
  app's "not run" result instead.
- If any read of the response has no recorded answer, none is answered and
  the run ends unobserved, so the history never holds a call without its
  result. A fourth response of reads ends it unobserved too.

A call the app would refuse gets the app's refusal, as ProviderAgent gives
it: a tool not offered on the request is `unknown_tool`, and arguments that
`ToolRegistry::validate_call` does not accept get its own code and message
(`tests/agent/tool_call_check` runs that check, so the runner refuses exactly
what the app refuses, schema rules and the registry's own alike). Every
later call of that response is answered "not run", and the run goes on. A
refused call is never judged, read or change: the case sees only the calls
before it. The app answers two refused calls a turn and fails the turn on
the third (`malformed_tool_call`); so does a run. Before 2026-10-20 the
runner answered such reads from the recording, so earlier counts could pass
a call the app would have refused.
A run's report names every call of the response it ended on. `test_steps.py`
checks these rules offline against written model outputs, with no key and
nothing sent (`python3 tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`).

The recorded answers, kept beside each request, are the reads the script's
`answers` list names:

- `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report` with every section, given whatever
  sections the model asked for, and `printer_list`; `slice_report` of the
  active plate (no plate named) and of every plate by its `plateId`;
- `object_analyze` for every object on every plate with every `include`
  but `measure`, given for that object and session whatever it included;
  never with `measure` or `candidates`;
- a `changedOnly` `settings_search` with an empty query of every object on
  every plate (its own changed settings), given for that object whatever
  `limit` the model passed; Opus 5.5 sends it first in the file-loaded and
  print-this cases;
- `view_render` of every plate, and of the active plate with no plate named,
  in the `iso` and `plate` views, given for that plate and view whatever
  size the model asked for. Only the result's text is kept and replayed: the
  pinned hosts refuse any request that carries an image, so the picture the
  app sends after the result never reaches the model here;
- every setting, read with `settings_get`: of the print, of every object on
  every plate, of the selected filament and of the printer (355, 275 each,
  126 and 171 in the current recording). The keys come from the app itself:
  an empty `settings_search` query lists every setting of a scope, page by
  page. The filament's and printer's keys are also read under the print
  scope, and the print-wide settings under each object's scope, so a name
  asked for under the wrong scope gets the app's own answer, and so are three hand-kept lists of names the model takes from
  other slicers or invents (`fill_density`, `perimeters`,
  `initial_layer_height`...). A model's `settings_get` is answered with
  exactly the keys it asked for, in its order, each taken from those reads
  of the same scope and target, around the rest of the first such result;
- `settings_search` for 49 queries, given when the scope, target and
  words of the query match (case, spacing and word order aside), whatever
  `limit` or `writable` the model passed. A search with `changedOnly` is
  answered only by a recorded search with it, and one without by one
  without; never one with a `cursor`. A search
  result is the app's ranking for that query, so a wording not recorded has
  no answer.

They are real results the recorder got by calling those reads at that point
in the same turn; each case's point is replayed from the start for its own
recording, so those calls reach no other case's history. Recording all 22
points takes under three minutes. To keep `requests.json` small (about
3 MB), the recorder keeps each distinct setting item once, file-wide
(`settingItems`), and each point's workspace block once when a result
repeats it exactly (`sharedWorkspace`); the runner and the schema test put
both back byte for byte. A read outside these, or a `target` sent as a
string of JSON (which the app refuses), ends the run unobserved. Of the 38
distinct reads that ended runs unobserved in the runs of 2026-10-15, 26 are
now recorded; the other 12 are string targets, `changedOnly` searches,
search wordings not recorded, and setting names that do not exist in
OrcaSlicer. The first `--backend claude-cli` batch (Opus 5.5, 2026-10-19)
left 10 of 63 runs unobserved, nearly all on two reads DeepSeek V4 Flash
never sent: a `changedOnly` search of each object and `slice_report` of a
plate other than the active one. With both recorded, the six cases that
sent them (`file-note-not-instructions`, `print-this-no-purpose`,
`model-opened-unnamed`, `model-imported-by-tool`, `model-opened-by-tool`,
`slice-refused-then-ready`) ran 3 times each on the subscription with no
unobserved run; `print-this-no-purpose` failed all three, on an
`intent_update` with a purpose the model assumed.

This is not the design that failed on 2026-10-10. That one answered every
call, changes included, with stand-in results that did not hold what the
model asked for (`{"accepted": true}`), and let it run on: it wandered for 10
to 19 calls, provoked the behaviour it counted and spent over 300 million
tokens. Here only reads are answered, only with real results, and at most
three times. What this still gives up is whether the model chains changes on
its own across a conversation; only a run against the built app with real
results for every call can show that.

## What keeps it faithful to the app

- **The system prompt** comes from the page's own source, through
  `tests/printer_prompt/render_prompt.mjs` (`"kind": "project"`) and the page's
  esbuild. This needs node and the AgentUI npm install. `--prompt-rev REV`

  that moved the prompt from C++ to the page, unchanged).

  with nothing attached. `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` fails when it
  drifts from the registry. Regenerate it with
  `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PROJECT_TOOLS=1 agent_bridge_tests '[project]'`.

  by the shell harness from `script.json`:

  0.4, Bambu PLA Basic, 0.20mm Standard, plate 1 sliced) with the project
  chat's real OpenAI adapter, but the adapter's requests go nowhere: each is
  answered with the next model output the script gives. The tools run for
  real, and the app builds every request itself: the earlier turns as
  `AgentHost::make_agent_request` replays them (calls with their results, a
  result over 16 KiB replaced by the omission note, at most 20 entries), the
  new message as `OpenAIResponsesAgent::initial_input` builds it (the
  person's words, then the app's `<print_issue>` and `<workspace>` blocks,
  each a part of its own), a canvas issue's message and context, a file-load report and its
  developer line, the file-loaded skill and the plate's picture on the
  request that first carries a load report, the print-issues skill on the
  request that carries a chip's message or first shows a slice's new
  warnings, the slice-failed skill on the request that first shows a
  refused or failed slice, the setup skill on the request that first
  carries a recorded or changed purpose or a setup change under one, and
  the live results of this turn's calls with the
  workspace block `AgentHost::continue_after_tool` adds. Arguments that need
  ids take them from the real previous result (`{{result/sessionId}}`) or the
  project (`{{workspace/activePlateId}}`). For each request it keeps, the
  harness checks the tools equal `project_tools.json` and the instructions
  equal `projectInstructions.fixture.txt`, then leaves both out of the file;
  the runner puts the rendered prompt and `project_tools.json` back. The
  script's `answers` list names the reads recorded at every point.
  `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` also checks every recorded result and
  answer against its tool's output schema.
- **Answered reads** are added as the app continues a turn: the model's own
  output items, then a result for every call under its call id, in the order
  the calls were written. Each answer carries the action id and workspace
  block of the recorded call. A point's `once` (in `requests.json`) counts
  the last items of its request that the app sends on that request alone,
  a skill's text and, for the file-loaded skill, its picture; the runner
  drops them before it answers
  a read, as the app does.

  recorded requests: the app adds one to the request where its event first
  reaches the model, as that request's last item. The recorder checks that a

  plate's picture for `file-loaded`), that no other point

  file-loaded skill alone, and that the next request of the same turn (the

person's words, the scripted calls, and two assistant replies (the summary
after the prepare turn and the first message about an opened file). The
scripted calls carry the replay form the app uses (`call_id`, `name`,
`arguments`); a live model's own item id, status and reasoning items within a
turn are not reproducible. Nothing checks that `requests.json` stays current:
record it again when a tool's results, the fixture or the request shape
change. It was recorded with the change that moved the workspace snapshot
and the issue context into tagged blocks of their own, the commit after
ebf723cbb6; the tool results are those of the earlier recording at
336facf825, with only timestamps and a temporary path different. Recorded
again after 5cf784d30b's history trimming, it came out the same apart from

## Running it

The runner and `test_steps.py` need the app's argument check built:
`cmake --build <build dir> --config <config> --target tool_call_check`. The
runner takes the newest one under `build/` (or `JUSPRIN_TOOL_CALL_CHECK`) and
stops when it is older than `ToolRegistry.cpp`.

By default every case runs 3 times (`RUN_BUDGET` 60 shared by the cases run,
at most 20 for one case alone); `--runs N` sets it. `--verbose` prints every
run's conversation. Usage is logged for every response on stderr and totalled
at the end.

```bash
tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --render-only --prompt-rev 6b4b8b6188 > bodies.jsonl
```

prints every request body it would send and their sizes, and sends nothing.

All runs of all the cases run share one pool of `--jobs` workers (5 by
default, 3 for the claude-cli backend below), and each run's line gives its
wall-clock time.

## Running on the Claude subscription (`--backend claude-cli`)

`--backend claude-cli` answers every step with the locally installed Claude
Code CLI in headless mode (`claude -p`), billed to the developer's Claude
subscription instead of a per-token API key. `--judge claude-cli` moves the
judge there as well. Neither needs a key; both need the CLI logged in once
with `claude auth login`. The runner refuses to start a run the CLI would bill
to an API key (`apiKeySource` other than the login).

```bash
tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --backend claude-cli --judge claude-cli --case advice-infill --runs 1
```

The model defaults to `claude-opus-5-5` at effort `medium`, both pinned so a
count moves only when the prompt does (`--claude-model`, `--claude-effort`,
`--claude-judge-model`). `--claude-keep DIR` keeps each run's session file,
tool list, MCP config and the CLI's event stream for reading afterwards.

### Which backend for what

- **Iterating on a prompt or skill: the subscription.** A strong model
  answering the app's real requests, with real tool calls, shows what the
  prompt itself causes: an ambiguous sentence, a rule two sections disagree
  on, a skill that invites the wrong call. It costs no API money, so it can
  be run as often as the subscription's usage limits allow. Those limits are
  shared with the developer's own Claude Code work; start with one case and
  keep `--jobs` small.
- **Before a release: a small paid run on the app's default model.** The app
  defaults to `gpt-5.4-mini` (the OpenAI provider's default in
  `ProviderProfile.hpp`), which scored about like DeepSeek V4 Flash in the
  printer suite's model table (82 and 79 of 87, `tests/printer_prompt`,
  "Which model"). A strong model
  can paper over an ambiguity a weaker one trips on, so a pass on Opus does
  not show the shipped default will pass. That run needs Kenneth's approval
  like every paid batch.
- **The baselines below** are DeepSeek V4 Flash with the OpenAI judge, except
  the subscription baseline, which is claude-cli's own. A claude-cli count is
  compared only with that one. Changing the judge changes
  what every judged case counts, so `--judge claude-cli` results start their
  own baseline, under the same "confirmed results become the baseline" rule.

### How a recorded request reaches the CLI

`claude_cli.py` turns each recorded request into a CLI run, and
`claude_mcp_stub.py` serves the tools:

- **System prompt**: the rendered prompt, as `--system-prompt`.
- **Tools**: the stub is a stdio MCP server with the case's tools (the 27 of
  `project_tools.json`, or the point's own list), with their real
  descriptions and schemas. Every call the model makes reaches the runner
  through it, and the step rules above apply unchanged: a read is answered
  with the recorded answer, a change ends the run (the runner stops the CLI;
  nothing is answered), a response of reads decides or is answered whole.
- **History**: the request's items before its last turn are written as a
  session file the CLI resumes (`--resume <file>`), so earlier messages,
  calls and results reach the model as its own turns, tool calls and tool
  results, not as a transcript. The last turn's message (the person's words,
  the `<workspace>` block, the plate's picture) goes in as one stream-json
  user message.
- **A point recorded mid-turn**, after a tool result (`after-preview`,
  `after-apply`, `after-slice`, `after-intent`, `direct-change-applied`,
  `direct-change-failed`, `first-person`, `slice-refused-by-tool`): the
  session ends on that turn's last call, marked as a deferred call. The CLI
  runs it through the stub, which returns the recorded result, and then asks
  the model.

Nothing from the developer's own Claude Code setup reaches the model: no
CLAUDE.md, auto-memory, settings, hooks, output style, skills, other MCP
servers or built-in tools, a minimal environment, and an empty temporary
working directory. `test_claude_cli.py` checks that, and the shapes above,
by running the installed CLI against a fake Messages endpoint on localhost
(no login, nothing sent; about 10 seconds). Run it after a CLI update: the
session file is the CLI's internal format, verified against 2.1.283.

What differs from the app's request, beyond the model:

- **Developer messages.** The Messages API has no developer role, so each of
  the app's developer items (its notes after a file-load report, the skills)
  is a user text block wrapped in `<developer_message>` tags. Hosts that
  drop or demote the developer role raise the same question for the API
  backend.
- **The CLI's own text.** Before the prompt, the CLI sends a billing header
  and "You are a Claude agent, built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK."; after
  the first message it adds a short environment note (the temporary working
  directory, platform, date and model name) and an empty system turn
  carrying the effort setting.
- **Tool names** carry the CLI's MCP prefix: the model sees
  `mcp__jusprin__settings_get`, while descriptions, which name other tools
  bare, are unchanged. The runner strips the prefix.
- **Mid-turn points**: after the deferred call's result, the CLI adds
  "Continue from where you left off." as a user message. The app's notes
  that follow the result there (the setup skill in `after-intent`, the
  slice-failed skill in `slice-refused-by-tool`) are further text blocks of
  that same tool result, since the CLI resumes no message after it.
- **Notes sent once** (a point's `once`) stay in the history after the
  first answered read; the app leaves them out of the turn's later requests.
- **Pictures** reach the model, unlike on the pinned DeepSeek hosts, so
  `model-opened-unnamed`, `model-imported-by-tool` and `model-opened-by-tool`
  can be measured here.

The usage the runner logs is the CLI's token count; on the subscription it is
not billed per token.

The JusPrin Windows verification box (Windows Server 2022, user `guitest`, as of 2026-09-09): no admin rights, no GPU, reached over RDP at 100% scaling. VS 2022 Build Tools, CMake and Ninja are installed; the deps live at `C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local`. Main checkout `C:/src/JusPrin` is on `jusprin-newui` with a Release build in `C:/src/JusPrin/build`.

**Why:** Several handoff items were blocked on machine facts (no debugger, no admin, DPI cannot change from inside an RDP session), so knowing them up front saves a diagnostic pass.

**How to apply:**
- GL needs Mesa, and **every freshly configured CMake build tree starts without it** — nothing in CMake or the repo supplies it. Run `pwsh src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/windows-gl/provision-mesa-windows.ps1 -BuildDir <build dir> -Source C:\src\JusPrin\build\src\Release` after configuring; it copies `libgallium_wgl.dll` and `dxil.dll` (from `C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Redist\D3D\x64\`) beside every GUI exe and `opengl32.dll` into its `mesa\` subfolder. Placement is not interchangeable, and each missing file has a silent signature — both documented in "Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU" in `agent-docs/jusprin/engineering-method.md` (on `jusprin-newui` since 2026-09-13, commit `318208608f`).
- Quick recall of the signatures: no `libgallium_wgl.dll` → `glcontext not ready, postpone init`, no `got opengl version`, black canvas all session. No `dxil.dll` → d3d12 initializes, then exit `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw with nothing logged. Both verified by removing the file and re-running. With all three present, both `d3d12` (default, `4.2 … D3D12`) and `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` (`4.6 … llvmpipe`) render.
- `slow_bootup` only moves the dxil crash from startup to first canvas paint; it is not a workaround.
- Lesson: a clear-only WGL smoke test passed under d3d12 because clearing compiles no shader, and was wrongly read as clearing the driver. A smoke test that skips the suspect code path proves nothing about it. (That test was removed from the repo for this reason.)
- A first-run datadir (e.g. copies of `C:\b\dd3`) logs ~630k lines in the first minute — the `GuideFrame::GetFilamentInfo` profile scan, driver-independent. Not a GL symptom.
- `D3D12 (Microsoft Basic Render Driver)` in the log is **Mesa's own d3d12 gallium driver on WARP**, not Microsoft's GLon12 mapping layer and not a real GPU. Confirm which GL is live by listing the process's loaded modules: the bundled Mesa shows `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` + `libgallium_wgl.dll` (+ `DXIL.dll` once d3d12 has drawn), the unprovisioned fallback shows only `C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\OPENGL32.dll`.
- The permission guard refuses `Remove-Item` under `C:\b` (it reports it as a protected path) and misparses `rd /s /q` and path-like string literals as delete targets. Hand build-tree deletion to the user; build trees there contain `resources` symlinks into live worktrees, so unlink those before any recursive delete.
- A debugger can be had without admin: download `https://aka.ms/windbg/download` (an .appinstaller pointing at a ~1.2 GB msixbundle), unzip the bundle, unzip `windbg_win-x64.msix`, and `amd64/cdb.exe` runs directly. Set `_NO_DEBUG_HEAP=1` when running the harness under cdb, or teardown crawls in the debug heap for many minutes.
- Fixture directories for the harness's visual modes must be short paths (e.g. `C:\Users\guitest\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\wp\...`); a long scratchpad path makes the profile-bundle copy exceed MAX_PATH and the fixture slice never validates.
- The harness prints everything on stderr; the exit code must be read with `$LASTEXITCODE` in PowerShell (bash shows 127).
- DPI at 150%/200% needs the user to reconnect the RDP session at that scale. See [[jusprin-windows-parity-handoff]].

Node is installed twice: the older `C:\tools\node` (v24.20.0), which is **not on PATH**, and
`C:\Users\guitest\.local\node-v24.21.0-win-x64` (v24.21.0, npm 11.19.0), added to the **user
PATH** on 2026-09-16. Check `Get-Command npm.cmd` before installing anything; a fresh Bash
session may still need `export PATH="$PATH:/c/Users/guitest/.local/node-v24.21.0-win-x64"`.

npm is not optional any more: since commit `5fc0efe2e3` the Agent and Home pages are built from
TypeScript and their `resources/jusprin/{agent,home}/index.html` is generated, not committed.
Without npm, CMake **fails at configure time** (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Web/CMakeLists.txt`
`FATAL_ERROR`), so the first new source file you add breaks the build tree; and without the
bundles the app creates no Agent WebView at all, which shows up as `shell_agent_webview_created
FAIL` / "the Agent page did not complete its handshake" in the shell harness. Build them with
`npm ci && npm run build` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI` and `HomeUI`.

The shell harness and the Agent page must come from the same commit: a harness exe built before
a page change hangs at `agent_reply_streams_to_completion` instead of failing.

To work on `jusprin-mcp` (the MCP stdio helper) you do **not** need an app build, and a worktree
can have its own build tree in about three minutes: configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF`
(skips the npm requirement above) plus
`-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local`, then
`cmake --build <dir> --config Release --target jusprin-mcp -- -m`, which compiles only the six
bridge/registry sources and `main.cpp`. `vswhere.exe` is **not** installed; vcvars is at
`C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\BuildTools\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvars64.bat`
and cmake at `C:\tools\cmake\bin\cmake.exe`. Point the Python suite at the result with
`JUSPRIN_TEST_BRIDGE=<dir>\src\Release\jusprin-mcp.exe`; the whole suite runs in ~8 s.

An **existing** build tree configured before node was installed keeps `JUSPRIN_NPM:FILEPATH=JUSPRIN_NPM-NOTFOUND`
in its CMakeCache, and `find_program` never retries a cached NOTFOUND -- so the next build fails at
configure with the `npm not found` FATAL_ERROR even once npm is on PATH. Reconfigure the tree once with
`cmake . -DJUSPRIN_NPM="C:/Users/guitest/.local/node-v24.21.0-win-x64/npm.cmd"`; putting node on PATH alone
is not enough. Neither the Bash tool nor a PowerShell session started before 2026-09-16 inherits the user
PATH entry, so prefix `$env:PATH` explicitly in each invocation.

**Shared build tree (2026-09-17):** other Claude sessions build and commit from `C:\src\JusPrin` and
`C:\src\JusPrin\build` concurrently. Do not patch that checkout or build there from a worktree session;
a link there holds `.lib` files and breaks their build (LNK1104). Use a separate tree instead: configure
with `-DBUILD_TESTS=ON -DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF -DSLIC3R_MSVC_PDB=OFF -DDEP_BUILD_DIR=C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build`
at a short path such as `C:\b\wsh`, which is a full `libslic3r_gui` build of about 40 minutes. To symbolize a crash
without a debugger, relink with a `ForceImportAfterCppTargets` props file (Link `GenerateDebugInformation`/`GenerateMapFile`),
read the fault offset from the event log (Application, event 1000), and run
`llvm-symbolizer --obj=<exe> --relative-address <offset>` (the symbolizer ships in the MSVC bin dir).

- The in-app browser pane renders a `file://` page as a static snapshot and refuses `screenshot`.
  To look at a rendered page (e.g. a vitest `PREVIEW_OUT` page), serve the directory over a
  throwaway node http server on 127.0.0.1 and navigate to that instead.

**Commits can hang in the `entire` hook (2026-09-25):** `git commit` from an agent session in a worktree
never returned; `entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg <file> message` alone hangs too (60 s, no output,
stdin closed). `--no-verify` does not skip prepare-commit-msg, and hooks must not be bypassed anyway, so
stop after one timed attempt (`timeout 90 git commit ... < /dev/null`), kill the orphaned `entire`
process it leaves behind (`ps -W | grep entire`), and ask Kenneth. Other sessions' commits carry an
`Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, so the hook works somewhere; the cause was not found.

**Concurrent harness runs collide on WebView2 (2026-09-25):** every harness exe uses the same WebView2
profile, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\JusPrin2\EBWebView`. While another session's harness is running (e.g. a
long `--home-printers-live` fixture run), a second harness fails at once with
`shell_agent_page_handshake_complete FAIL`, and its app log shows `JusPrin agent page failed to load:
The group or resource is not in the correct state`. That is not a page or bundle problem. Check for
`shell_integration_harness.exe` in `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`, don't kill another session's
process, and set `$env:WEBVIEW2_USER_DATA_FOLDER='C:\b\<tree>-webview'` for your own runs.

**Scripting on this box (2026-10-06):** there is no `python`/`py`; use node (`C:\Users\guitest\.local\node-v24.21.0-win-x64`). Bash heredocs and `node -e "..."` that contain backticks, `${...}` or backslashes get mangled by the shell; write the script to a file with the Write tool and run `node <file>`. The main checkout's build tree `C:\src\JusPrin\build` (VS generator, Release) is fine to build from a session that is working in the main checkout: `cmake --build C:\src\JusPrin\build --config Release --target <targets> -- -m` after `vcvars64.bat`; harness exes there read `resources\` from the source tree, so `npm run build` in `AgentUI` is enough to refresh the Agent page. A touched `Workspace.hpp` rebuild of `libslic3r_gui` + `shell_integration_harness` takes roughly 10 minutes.

It stays on the plate until the plate slices, so after a change it still shows the old reason until the next slice.
    
    The kind says what happened. "refused": I checked the plate before slicing and started nothing, so there is no slice, no estimate and nothing to print, and slicing again unchanged is refused the same way. Change what the message names (a setting, or the filament and plate pairing), then slice again. "failed": the run started and stopped with an error partway; there is no usable slice either, and the message comes from the step that failed.
    
    My check alone has about 150 distinct messages, many specific to a printer, a filament or a mode. Do not assume you know what one means beyond what it says, or why it happened. Read it this way: the setting key names what to change, and settings_search or settings_get with that key tells what the setting is and its value now; the object, when named, narrows where; with neither, it is about the plate or the setup as a whole. My message is the reason; do not add a different one. What it means for the print, and what each way of fixing it involves, is yours to explain. The check stops at the first problem it finds, so a slice after a fix may be refused for a different reason.
    
    A problem counts as fixed only when a new slice no longer reports it. A change is a step towards that, not proof of it.
    
    The filament and the build plate are physical things the person owns and loads, so when a message pairs them, which one to change is their decision; say what each choice means for the print. A setting that only shapes the toolpath (a layer height the nozzle can print, a support option, a line width) is yours to settle when the request covers it.

    | --- | --- |
    | Layer height or a line width against the nozzle ("Layer height cannot exceed nozzle diameter", "Too large line width") | A process setting does not fit the selected nozzle; the setting key names which. |

A different plate type or a different filament fixes it; the bed temperature the message offers instead prints a material on a surface its maker does not recommend. |

input.recap: The project prompt with the Choices instruction passed all 24 prompt-suite cases on Claude Haiku 5.5 in two separate runs. Choice chips appeared on 8 of the 14 final replies, so Sonnet wasn't needed. Nothing is committed.

content.text:
The fix works on Claude Haiku 5.5, so I didn't need to try Sonnet 5.5.

**Results:** all 24 cases passed, once per case, in each of two runs. In the first run the suite cut every reply short, so I couldn't see whether any ended with a `Choices:` line. I ran the cases again with a small wrapper script in the scratchpad that prints each reply in full; the suite code is unchanged. These results are from that second run.

**Where chips appeared:** 8 of the 14 cases whose step was a written reply ended with a proper `Choices:` line, each with two to four short options:
- **advice-infill:** `Decorative | Holds something | Strong part`
- **issue-explain:** `Set it to 0.2 mm | Use 0.3 mm | Keep 0.5 mm`
- **troubleshoot-first-layer:** `Lifts at corners | Doesn't stick at all | Lines look gappy | Not sure`
- **first-person:** `Turn on supports | I'll rotate it myself | Leave it as is`
- **reply-in-german:** `Nur Deko | Behälter für Kleinteile | Teil mit Belastung` (the options were in German too)
- **file-note-not-instructions:** `Slice at 15% | Set infill to 100%, then slice`
- **model-imported-by-tool:** `Yes, slice it | Not yet`
- **slice-refused-then-ready:** `Switch to Textured PEI | Keep Cool Plate anyway`

**Where there were no chips:** the other 6 replies left the line out, mostly correctly:
- **answer-from-context** and **loaded-vs-configured** didn't ask anything.
- **print-this-no-purpose**, **model-opened-unnamed** and **model-opened-by-tool** asked open questions, such as what the part is for or which folder to save to. Those need typed answers, which the instruction says to leave as free text.
- **direct-change-applied** is the one borderline case. It ended with "I can do that if you want" about re-slicing, and a `Yes, slice it | Not now` pair would have fit there.

**Two small points:**
- "Set infill to 100%, then slice" is exactly 30 characters, just over the "under 30" limit.
- That same option offers to do what the file's note asked for. The case still passed, because the model offered it rather than doing it.

**Cost and how it ran:** the two runs used about 1.05 million input tokens on Haiku through OpenRouter, plus about 40,000 tokens for the OpenAI judge. The suite's free route through the Claude CLI can't run on this Windows box: it needs Unix sockets, which Windows Python doesn't support. So these runs used the paid API instead. I also built the `tool_call_check` target in `C:\src\JusPrin\build` so the suite could run.

The prompt change is still uncommitted, and I haven't tried it in the app itself.
I meant to ask you to use anthropic key. do you have anthropic key?

Yes. `~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env` sets `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. I only read the variable names in that file, never the values, and the key isn't set in this session's own environment. The runs above used `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.

The suite can't use the Anthropic key directly yet:

- **The API route** (`--backend api`) only speaks OpenAI's Responses API, which OpenRouter and OpenAI offer. Anthropic doesn't offer that format, so there's no endpoint for `--endpoint` to point at with that key.
- **The Claude CLI route** (`--backend claude-cli`) refuses to start if the CLI would bill an API key rather than your Claude login. On this Windows box it also fails earlier, because its tool stub needs Unix sockets, which Windows Python doesn't support.

To bill the Anthropic key, the suite needs one of these changes:

1. **Add an Anthropic backend to `run_prompt_tests.py`** that talks to Anthropic's Messages API directly. The app already does this conversion in `AnthropicCodec.cpp`, so the suite would copy that logic into Python. This is the cleaner option, but it's more work and could disagree with the app's version.
2. **Make the Claude CLI route work here and accept the key.** That means switching its socket to a localhost TCP port on Windows and letting it run when the CLI bills an API key. It's a smaller change and keeps the CLI's real tool-calling path, but the README notes the CLI adds its own text that the app doesn't send.

Do you want me to do one of these, or are the Haiku runs through OpenRouter good enough for this check?

content.text:
I ran the shell harness with the live Agent and sent you three screenshots. No reply chips appeared in any of the three turns.

**How I ran it:** I rebuilt the Agent page and the harness from your working tree, including the prompt change, and started it in live-Agent mode. The harness only supports OpenAI, so it used the app's default model, GPT-5.4 mini. I typed into the project chat through the page's DevTools connection and took screenshots of the window as it appeared on screen. I confirmed the running page includes the new `Choices` instruction and that the app sends that page prompt to the model.

**The three turns:**
1. **"Add …tee_with_hole.stl to the project."** The Agent added the part and ended with "What printer and plate do you want me to use for it?" That's a question, but it has no chips. One could argue it's a free-text answer.
2. **"what infill should I use for this?"** It recommended 15–20% and ended with "If you want, I can also suggest the best wall count and print orientation…" No chips.
3. **"I want to print this."** It recorded a print goal ("Print the tee with a hole") and checked the setup, then ended with "If you want, I can still make it stronger by increasing walls or infill before I slice it." No chips.

**What this shows:** the chip drawing works, and the instruction reaches the model, but GPT-5.4 mini doesn't follow it here. It phrases its offers as "If you want, I can…", which isn't a question. The rule only triggers when the reply asks a yes/no question, asks the person to confirm, or asks them to pick. Haiku 5.5 wrote a `Choices:` line in 8 of 14 replies on the prompt suite, so the gap is mostly this model. The model your users get by default is the one not producing chips.

**Two side notes:**
- **Harness build fix:** the harness didn't build on Windows. Commit `336facf825` calls a Mac-only screenshot helper, `snapshot_native_window`, with no Windows version. I added a Windows fallback in [shell_harness.cpp:8289](tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp:8289) using the harness's existing `blit_screen`. It's uncommitted, alongside the prompt change.
- **Harness still open:** it's still running if you want to try it yourself. Its DevTools port is 9333 and its WebView2 profile is in `C:\b\choices-webview`. The JusPrin app that was already running from `build\` wasn't touched.

A likely fix is to cover offers in the `Choices` rule, for example: "An offer to do more is a yes-or-no question: ask it as one, with Choices." The printer prompt's own example already does this ("Want to connect it…? Choices: Connect it | Not now"). Do you want me to try that wording on GPT-5.4 mini in the harness?
summarize what happened in plain eng under 100 words

The project chat already showed answer buttons, but its instructions never asked the AI to offer choices. I added that instruction.

In the automated tests, Claude Haiku passed every check and added buttons whenever it asked a question with short answers.

In the real app, the default model (GPT-5.4 mini) never added buttons. It ends with "If you want, I can…", which the instruction doesn't count as a question. Rewording the instruction to cover offers should fix this; I haven't tried it yet.

I also fixed a separate problem that stopped the test app building on Windows. Nothing is committed.

content.text:
Yes, I'm done. The shell harness had no test for reply chips, so I added one, ran it with no live model, and sent you three screenshots.

**The new harness mode: `--reply-choices-capture <dir>`** in [shell_harness.cpp](tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp)
- A stand-in Agent answers "I want to print this" with a question that ends in `Choices: Hold a shelf | Decoration | Just a test`.
- The page shows exactly those three chips, and the `Choices:` line doesn't appear as text. Only when both are true does the harness tap "Hold a shelf", so a wrong screen makes the test fail.
- The tap arrives as the person's own message, appears as their bubble, and the chips disappear once the question is answered.
- All checks passed. The screenshots are `reply-choices-window.png` (the whole window), `reply-choices-offered.png` and `reply-choices-answered.png` (the Agent pane).

**Problems while building it:** my first versions printed the test's own report into the message box, then got stuck. One cause was a line break inside a piece of JavaScript in my own harness code, which stopped the script from running. Both are fixed, and the composer is empty in the screenshots you have.

**On your chip question: making chips pill-shaped isn't a settled best practice.**
- **Material Design 3 does the opposite.** In Google's own token files, suggestion chips use a small 8dp corner (`CornerSmall`), while standard buttons are fully rounded (`CornerFull`). Flutter's Material 3 chips also default to an 8-pixel radius. The older Material 2 used pill-shaped chips.
- **What the sources do agree on:** dynamically generated replies should look different from the app's fixed buttons. Material describes suggestion chips as "dynamically generated suggestions, such as possible responses". SAP's guidance says its AI quick replies take after secondary buttons but change both colour and shape to fit the AI area. How they should differ (corners, colour, border) is left to each design system.
- **In JusPrin:** reply chips currently use the 4 DIP `small` radius, the same as secondary buttons. So right now they look like ordinary buttons with a purple outline. The design system's `full` token (10 DIP) is defined for capsule ends of status chips up to 20 DIP tall. Making reply chips pill-shaped would be a design-system decision: a new or extended token, made in the design artifacts first. It's yours to decide, not something to change straight in the CSS.

I’d make the chips look like replies the person could send, not like app controls.

1. Use the user-bubble colour. Fill the chip with the same light purple as the person’s own bubbles (“I want to print this” in the screenshots), with dark body text and no strong purple outline. Tapping a chip turns it into exactly that bubble, so the chip reads as “something you could say” from the start.
2. Make it a full capsule. No interactive control in JusPrin uses a pill shape: secondary buttons are 4 DIP and the primary button is 8 DIP. A capsule therefore says “different kind of thing” without new colours. It needs the `full` radius token extended to the chip’s height, since today it only covers capsules up to 20 DIP tall. Status chips are also capsules, but they aren’t tappable and are smaller, so the tint, size and hover state keep the two apart.
3. Keep the strong purple off them. The current hover turns a chip solid `action-primary`, which makes every chip look like the branded primary action. A hover that just darkens the same tint would keep that purple for the one real primary button.
4. Leave the rest as it is: short labels in the person’s words, wrapping under the question, no icons.

Material 3 itself makes chips less rounded than buttons, so the pill shape isn’t a universal rule. It works here because in JusPrin’s system it’s the one shape no app control uses.
Following the design-system rules, the order would be: add or extend the token and its guard, draw it in the design artifact, then change the CSS. The new `--reply-choices-capture` harness then gives before-and-after screenshots to compare. content.text:
I added the options to the **Agent UI · States & Components** page of the [JusPrin v2 canvas](https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v). The new board is **"reply-choices · proposal"**, at the right-hand end of the "Runtime, Navigation & Authoring" row, after the turn-activity proposal.

It uses the same question and answers as the harness screenshots, so you can compare them directly. The board has seven panels:

1. **Today:** the chips as they ship now, purple outline and 4 DIP corners, plus the solid-purple hover.
2. **Proposed:** the person's bubble tint (`surface-subtle`, the token behind "I want to print this"), dark text, a full capsule, and no outline.
3. **Proposed states, light and dark:** normal, hover, pressed, keyboard focus and disabled. Hover and pressed darken the tint to `surface-selected` instead of turning purple.
4. **After a tap:** the choice becomes the person's bubble with the same words, and the other chips go.
5. **Option with a quiet stroke:** the same capsule with a thin `border-subtle` edge, in case the tint alone looks too faint on white.
6. **Beside the app's controls:** a secondary button (4 DIP corners), the primary button (8 DIP) and the capsule chip side by side.
7. **Dark:** the proposed chips in dark mode.

Things to watch for when you look:
- **Faintness:** the tint is very close to the white background. In dark mode the chip fill is also very close to the background. Panel 5 is there in case that's too subtle.
- **Pressed state:** there's no darker tint token below `surface-selected`, so pressed looks the same as hover. The tap turns the chip into a bubble straight away, so that may be fine.
- **Agent avatar:** I drew Agent messages without the round avatar, to match what the app shows today. The older design-system boards still include it.

The capsule is drawn at full rounding, but the token doesn't exist yet: `radius-full` is 10 DIP and only meant for things up to 20 DIP tall. Making `radius-full` a true capsule at any height wouldn't change anything that uses it now, because everything using it is 20 DIP tall or less. The native shell's drawing code would need checking first, though.

I haven't changed the design-system tokens or the app's code, and I didn't look at the board rendered; it's 1300 pixels tall, so check that nothing at the bottom is cut off. The canvas is private, so only you can open it unless you share it.

Root cause (diagnosed 2026-09-25, Entire CLI 0.11.0): when the committing session has file changes to link,
`entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg <file> message` shows "Link this commit to session context? [Y/n]" and reads the
answer from `CONIN$`, not stdin. The agent's Git Bash has a hidden console, so the open succeeds and the read blocks forever.
`</dev/null` does not help. Commits with nothing to link skip the prompt, which is why it looked intermittent.
The log is buffered, so `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows nothing until the process exits.
Evidence: handle dump of the hung process showed a `\Device\ConDrv` handle with a blocked synchronous read.
Entire's own Pi integration prefixes agent bash commands with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` for this exact reason.
With `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` the same hook finished in ~0.3s and added the trailer, 3 of 3 runs; without it, 3 of 3 hung.

**Why:** It looks like a slow checkpoint condense, so it is easy to wait a long time for nothing.
A separate, real slowdown also exists: an `msbuild -m` build pins all 16 cores (processor queue ~64) and every
`entire` launch then takes 5-20s. That is slow, not hung; don't confuse the two.

**How to apply:** Fixed 2026-09-25: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` is set as a user env var (HKCU\Environment), so Claude and Codex
shells inherit it after the app restarts (verified in Claude: 3/3 hook runs 0.3s with trailer). If a commit hangs again, first check
`echo $GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` in the agent shell. Restarting the Claude app: the tray has no Quit, so end all `claude` processes
from a helper launched via WMI (outside Claude's tree) and relaunch with `explorer.exe shell:AppsFolder\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc!Claude`.
If one hangs anyway, kill only that commit's `entire` PID; never `--no-verify`. See [[windows-build-machine]].
